slides.title: Your moka is done sooner than you think
slides.subtitle: One sound tells you when to stop. Most people wait past it.

slides.myth: Leave the moka pot on the heat until it stops.
slides.truth: The last stream is paler and more bitter. Most guides say to pull the pot off the heat at the first sputter.

slides.title: What the sputter means
slides.body: Gurgling and sputtering mark the end of the good coffee. The stream turns pale, almost honey-colored, and what follows tastes more bitter.

slides.title: Heat lingers after the flame
slides.body: A hot pot keeps pushing water through the coffee even off the stove. Run the base under cold tap water to stop it.

slides.title: How to stop in time
steps: Use low to medium heat, lid open.
Watch the stream, not the clock.
Pull the pot at the first sputter.
Cool the base under cold water.

slides.label: The tip
slides.body: If you hear sputtering, you are already a few seconds late. Pull the pot when the stream turns honey-colored, then taste and adjust.

slides.title: Stop at the first sputter
slides.body: Pale stream, sputter, off the heat. Then cool the base.
